claim: Visual speech carried by lip movements is an integral part of communication.
source: Visual speech carried by lip movements is an integral part of communication.
evidence: This is a general statement about communication that draws from established scientific understanding.

claim: It remains unclear in how far visual and acoustic speech comprehension are mediated by the same brain regions.
source: Yet, it remains unclear in how far visual and acoustic speech comprehension are mediated by the same brain regions.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field and identifies a gap in understanding.

claim: The comprehension-relevant representations of auditory and visual speech converged only in anterior angular and inferior frontal regions.
source: The comprehension-relevant representations of auditory and visual speech converged only in anterior angular and inferior frontal regions and were spatially dissociated from those representations that best reflected the sensory-driven word identity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental results from MEG data analysis presented in the study.

claim: Comprehension-relevant representations of auditory and visual speech were spatially dissociated from those representations that best reflected the sensory-driven word identity.
source: The comprehension-relevant representations of auditory and visual speech converged only in anterior angular and inferior frontal regions and were spatially dissociated from those representations that best reflected the sensory-driven word identity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental results comparing stimulus classification and neurobehavioral prediction.

claim: Cerebral representations encoding word identities may be more modality-specific than often upheld.
source: These results provide a neural explanation for the behavioural dissociation of acoustic and visual speech comprehension and suggest that cerebral representations encoding word identities may be more modality-specific than often upheld.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and analysis presented in the study.

claim: Movements of the mouth, lips and tongue provide both redundant and complementary information to acoustic cues.
source: Movements of the mouth, lips and tongue in particular provide both redundant and complementary information to acoustic cues (Hall et al., 2005; Peelle and Sommers, 2015; Plass et al., 2019; Summerfield, 1992)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Visual speech can help to enhance speech intelligibility in noisy environments and in a second language.
source: and can help to enhance speech intelligibility in noisy environments and in a second language (Navarra and Soto-Faraco, 2007; Sumby and Pollack, 1954; Yi et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Performance in auditory/verbal and visual speech comprehension tasks are uncorrelated in the typical adult population.
source: In the typical adult population, performance in auditory/verbal and visual speech comprehension tasks are uncorrelated (Conrad, 1977; Jeffers and Barley, 1980; Mohammed et al., 2006; Summerfield, 1991; Summerfield, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous behavioral studies.

claim: Large inter-individual differences in lip reading skills contrast with the low variability seen in auditory speech tests.
source: Moreover, large inter-individual differences in lip reading skills contrast with the low variability seen in auditory speech tests (Summerfield, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Neuroimaging and neuroanatomical studies have suggested the convergence of acoustic and visual speech information in specific brain regions.
source: In contrast to this behavioural dissociation, neuroimaging and neuroanatomical studies have suggested the convergence of acoustic and visual speech information in specific brain regions (Calvert, 1997; Campbell, 2008; Ralph et al., 2017; Simanova et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous neuroimaging studies.

claim: A fronto-temporal network mediates acoustic speech representations, comprising a word-meaning pathway from auditory cortex to inferior frontal areas, and an articulatory pathway that extends from auditory to motor regions.
source: Prevalent models postulate a fronto-temporal network mediating acoustic speech representations, comprising a word-meaning pathway from auditory cortex to inferior frontal areas, and an articulatory pathway that extends from auditory to motor regions (Giordano et al., 2017; Giraud and Poeppel, 2012; Gross et al., 2013; Hickok, 2012; Huth et al., 2016; Morillon et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous models and studies.

claim: Anterior-temporal and frontal regions have been implied in implementing a-modal semantic representations.
source: Specifically, a number of anterior-temporal and frontal regions have been implied in implementing a-modal semantic representations (MacSweeney et al., 2008; Ralph et al., 2017; Simanova et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Visual speech activates ventral and dorsal visual pathways and bilateral fronto-temporal circuits.
source: Previous studies have shown that visual speech activates ventral and dorsal visual pathways and bilateral fronto-temporal circuits (Bernstein and Liebenthal, 2014; Calvert, 1997; Campbell, 2008; Capek et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Some studies have explicitly suggested that auditory regions are also involved in lip reading.
source: Some studies have explicitly suggested that auditory regions are also involved in lip reading (Calvert, 1997; Calvert and Campbell, 2003; Capek et al., 2008; Lee and Noppeney, 2011; Pekkola et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Visual cortices can send signals to auditory regions that can be exploited to establish coarse-grained acoustic representations.
source: for example by receiving signals from visual cortices that can be exploited to establish coarse-grained acoustic representations (Bourguignon et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Most studies focused on mapping activations rather than specific semantic or lexical speech content.
source: This is in part because most studies focused on mapping activations rather than specific semantic or lexical speech content.
evidence: This is an observation about the methodological approach of previous studies.

claim: Alternative accounts have been proposed which hold that visual and auditory speech representations are largely distinct.
source: Indeed, alternative accounts have been proposed, which hold that visual and auditory speech representations are largely distinct (Bernstein and Liebenthal, 2014; Evans et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: It is important to distinguish purely stimulus driven neural activity from activity specifically representing a stimulus and contributing to the participant's percept on an individual trial.
source: When investigating how speech is encoded in the brain, it is important to distinguish purely stimulus driven neural activity (e.g. classic 'activation') from activity specifically representing a stimulus and contributing to the participant's percept on an individual trial (Bouton et al., 2018; Grootswagers et al., 2018; Keitel et al., 2018; Panzeri et al., 2017; Tsunada et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous methodological studies.

claim: Cerebral representations representing the physical speech are partly distinct from those reflecting the actually perceived meaning.
source: Recent neuroimaging studies have suggested that those cerebral representations representing the physical speech are partly distinct from those reflecting the actually perceived meaning.
evidence: This claim is supported by the context of recent neuroimaging studies.

claim: Syllable identity can be decoded from temporal, occipital and frontal areas, but only focal activity in the inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) and posterior superior temporal gyrus (pSTG) mediates perceptual categorisation.
source: For example, syllable identity can be decoded from temporal, occipital and frontal areas, but only focal activity in the inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) and posterior superior temporal gyrus (pSTG) mediates perceptual categorisation (Bouton et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The encoding of the acoustic speech envelope is seen widespread in the brain, but correct word comprehension correlates only with focal activity in temporal and motor regions.
source: Similarly, the encoding of the acoustic speech envelope is seen widespread in the brain, but correct word comprehension correlates only with focal activity in temporal and motor regions (Scott, 2019; Keitel et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Activity in lower sensory pathways seems to correlate more with the actual physical stimulus, while activity in specific higher-tier regions correlates with the subjective percept.
source: In general, activity in lower sensory pathways seems to correlate more with the actual physical stimulus, while activity in specific higher-tier regions correlates with the subjective percept (Crochet et al., 2019; Romo et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Participants performed a comprehension task based on individual sentences that were presented either acoustically or visually (lip reading), while brain activity was recorded using MEG.
source: To this end, we exploited a paradigm in which participants performed a comprehension task based on individual sentences that were presented either acoustically or visually (lip reading), while brain activity was recorded using MEG (Keitel et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: Participants perceived the correct target word in approximately 70% of trials across auditory and visual conditions.
source: On average, participants perceived the correct target word in approximately 70% of trials across auditory and visual conditions (chance level was 25%).
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the experiment.

claim: The behavioural performance did not differ significantly between auditory and visual conditions.
source: The behavioural performance did not differ significantly between these conditions (Mauditory = 69.7%, SD = 7.1%, Mvisual = 71.7%, SD = 20.0%; t(19) = −0.42, p=0.68; Figure 1)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: The addition of acoustic background noise equalised performance between auditory and visual conditions.
source: demonstrating that the addition of acoustic background noise indeed equalised performance between conditions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral results.

claim: The between-subject variability in performance was larger in the visual condition (between 31.7% and 98.3%).
source: Still, the between-subject variability in performance was larger in the visual condition (between 31.7% and 98.3%), in line with the notion that lip reading abilities vary considerably across individuals (Bernstein and Liebenthal, 2014; Summerfield, 1992; Tye-Murray et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the experiment, supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Participants' behavioural responses were influenced by both semantic and phonological features in both conditions.
source: An explorative representational similarity analysis (RSA) (Evans and Davis, 2015; Kriegeskorte et al., 2008) indicated that participants' behavioural responses were influenced by both semantic and phonological features in both conditions (see Materials and methods, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the representational similarity analysis.

claim: In both conditions phonological features influenced behaviour stronger than semantic features.
source: A post-hoc comparison revealed that in both conditions phonological features influenced behaviour stronger than semantic features (Wilcoxon Signed-ranks test; Zauditory = 151, p=0.037, Zvisual = 189, p=0.002).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the representational similarity analysis.

claim: Auditory speech was represented bilaterally in fronto-temporal areas, extending into intra-parietal regions within the left hemisphere.
source: Auditory speech was represented bilaterally in fronto-temporal areas, extending into intra-parietal regions within the left hemisphere (Figure 2A; Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the MEG source activity classification analysis, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Visual speech was represented bilaterally in occipital areas, as well as in left parietal and frontal areas.
source: Visual speech was represented bilaterally in occipital areas, as well as in left parietal and frontal areas (Figure 2B), with classification performance between 25.9% and 33.9%.
evidence: This is a result from the MEG source activity classification analysis, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The regions representing word identity in both visual and auditory conditions overlapped in the middle and inferior temporal gyrus, the postcentral and supramarginal gyri, and the left inferior frontal gyrus.
source: The regions representing word identity in both visual and auditory conditions overlapped in the middle and inferior temporal gyrus, the postcentral and supramarginal gyri, and the left inferior frontal gyrus (Figure 2C; overlap in green).
evidence: This is a result from the MEG source activity classification analysis, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Both auditory clusters and the occipital visual cluster contained grid points with substantial or strong evidence for a significant modality difference.
source: However, both auditory clusters and the occipital visual cluster contained grid points with substantial or strong (bf10 > 3 and bf10 > 10, respectively) evidence for a significant modality difference.
evidence: This is a result from the Bayes factor analysis comparing auditory and visual word classification.

claim: The visual postcentral region (POST), the IFG and the overlap region contained many grid points with substantial evidence for no difference between modalities.
source: In contrast, the visual postcentral region (POST), the IFG and the overlap region contained many grid points with substantial evidence for no difference between modalities (1∕10 < bf10<1∕3).
evidence: This is a result from the Bayes factor analysis comparing auditory and visual word classification.

claim: Auditory classification was significantly better in clusters covering left and right auditory cortices.
source: Auditory classification was significantly better in clusters covering left and right auditory cortices, while visual classification was significantly better in bilateral visual sensory areas.
evidence: This is a result from the full-brain cluster-based permutation test for modality difference.

claim: Visual classification was significantly better in bilateral visual sensory areas.
source: Auditory classification was significantly better in clusters covering left and right auditory cortices, while visual classification was significantly better in bilateral visual sensory areas.
evidence: This is a result from the full-brain cluster-based permutation test for modality difference.

claim: There was evidence for a statistically significant lateralisation for both auditory clusters.
source: We found evidence for a statistically significant lateralisation for both auditory clusters (left cluster peaking in POST: t(17) = 5.15, pFDR <0.001; right cluster peaking in RO: t(17) = 4.26, pFDR <0.01).
evidence: This is a result from the lateralisation test.

claim: In the auditory condition, five distinct clusters showed neural representations of word identity predictive of behaviour.
source: In the auditory condition, we found five distinct clusters. Three were in the left hemisphere, peaking in the left inferior temporal gyrus (left ITG; Tsum = 469.55, p<0.001), the inferior frontal gyrus (left IFG; Tsum = 138.70, p<0.001), and the middle occipital gyrus (left MOG; Tsum = 58.44, p<0.001). In the right hemisphere, the two significant clusters were in the supplementary motor area (right SMA; Tsum = 312.48, p<0.001) and in the angular gyrus (right AG; Tsum = 68.59, p<0.001; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a result from the neurobehavioral analysis, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In the visual condition, four clusters showed neural representations of word identity predictive of behaviour.
source: In the visual condition, we found four clusters: A left-hemispheric cluster in the inferior frontal gyrus (left IFG; Tsum = 144.15, p<0.001) and three clusters with right-hemispheric peaks, in the superior temporal gyrus (right STG; Tsum = 168.68, p<0.001), the superior frontal gyrus (right SFG; Tsum = 158.39, p<0.001) and the angular gyrus (right AG; Tsum = 37.42, p<0.001; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a result from the neurobehavioral analysis, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Perception-relevant auditory and visual representations did not overlap.
source: Interestingly, these perception-relevant (i.e. predictive) auditory and visual representations did not overlap (Figure 3C), although some of them occurred in adjacent regions in the IFG and AG.
evidence: This is a result from the neurobehavioral analysis, shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Three auditory clusters contained grid points that differed substantially or strongly between modalities (left ITG, left MOG, and right AG).
source: Three auditory clusters contained grid points that differed substantially or strongly (bf10 > 3 and bf10 > 10, respectively) between modalities (left ITG, left MOG, and right AG).
evidence: This is a result from the Bayes factor analysis of neurobehavioral prediction.

claim: In two regions the majority of grid points provided substantial evidence for no difference between modalities (IFG and AG from the visual condition).
source: In addition, in two regions the majority of grid points provided substantial evidence for no difference between modalities (IFG and AG from the visual condition).
evidence: This is a result from the Bayes factor analysis of neurobehavioral prediction.

claim: There was evidence for a significant modality specialisation for auditory words in four clusters in the left middle occipital gyrus, left calcarine gyrus, right posterior angular gyrus, and bilateral supplementary motor area.
source: A separate full-brain cluster-based permutation test (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) provided evidence for a significant modality specialisation for auditory words in four clusters in the left middle occipital gyrus, left calcarine gyrus, right posterior angular gyrus, and bilateral supplementary motor area.
evidence: This is a result from the full-brain cluster-based permutation test for modality difference in neurobehavioral prediction.

claim: Regions predictive of visual word comprehension did not show a significant modality preference.
source: On the other hand, regions predictive of visual word comprehension did not show a significant modality preference.
evidence: This is a result from the full-brain cluster-based permutation test for modality difference in neurobehavioral prediction.

claim: No evidence was found for significant cross-classification between auditory and visual conditions at the whole-brain level.
source: At the whole-brain level, we found no evidence for significant cross-classification (two-sided cluster-based permutation statistics, neither at a corrected p=0.001 nor a more lenient p=0.05; Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, left panel).
evidence: This is a result from the cross-decoding analysis.

claim: Most grid points contained substantial evidence for no cross-classification between the auditory and visual conditions.
source: An analysis of the Bayes factors for this cross-classification test confirmed that most grid points contained substantial evidence for no cross-classification between the auditory and visual conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B, left panel).
evidence: This is a result from the Bayes factor analysis of cross-classification.

claim: There was strong evidence for significant cross-classification between the uni- and multisensory conditions in temporal and occipital regions.
source: On the other hand, there was strong evidence for significant cross-classification between the uni- and multisensory conditions in temporal and occipital regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B, right panel).
evidence: This is a result from the Bayes factor analysis of cross-classification.

claim: Brain regions in which sensory representations shape speech comprehension are mostly distinct from those allowing the best prediction of the actual stimulus.
source: The above results suggest that the brain regions in which sensory representations shape speech comprehension are mostly distinct from those allowing the best prediction of the actual stimulus (see Figure 4 for direct visualisation of the results from both analyses).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing stimulus classification and neurobehavioral prediction results.

claim: Only parts of the left inferior temporal gyrus (auditory condition), the right superior temporal gyrus (visual condition) and the left inferior frontal gyrus (both conditions) feature high stimulus classification and a driving role for comprehension.
source: Only parts of the left inferior temporal gyrus (auditory condition), the right superior temporal gyrus (visual condition) and the left inferior frontal gyrus (both conditions) feature high stimulus classification and a driving role for comprehension.
evidence: This is a result from comparing stimulus classification and neurobehavioral prediction.

claim: The accuracy by which local activity reflects the physical stimulus is generally not predictive of the impact of this local word representation on behaviour.
source: In other words, the accuracy by which local activity reflects the physical stimulus is generally not predictive of the impact of this local word representation on behaviour.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the regression analysis between stimulus classification and neurobehavioral weights.

claim: Group-level statistics of the participant-specific beta values provided no support for a consistent relationship between overall stimulus classification performance and the perceptual weight of each local representation across all grid points.
source: Group-level statistics of the participant-specific beta values provided no support for a consistent relationship between these (auditory condition: b = 0.05 ± 0.11 [M ± SEM], t(17) = 0.50, pFDR = 0.81; visual condition: b = 0.03 ± 0.11 [M ± SEM], t(14) = 0.25, pFDR = 0.81; participant-specific regression slopes are depicted in Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a result from the regression analysis between stimulus classification and neurobehavioral weights.

claim: Stimulus classification performance was not significantly correlated with behavioural performance across participants.
source: We found no significant clusters (all ps > 0.11, two-sided cluster-based permutation statistics, uncorrected across the four tests), indicating that stimulus classification performance was not significantly correlated with behavioural performance across participants (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a result from the correlation analysis between stimulus classification and behavioral performance.

claim: In the large majority of brain regions, there is substantial evidence for no correlation between stimulus classification performance and behavioral performance.
source: The corresponding Bayes factors confirm that in the large majority of brain regions, there is substantial evidence for no correlation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a result from the Bayes factor analysis of correlations between stimulus classification and behavioral performance.

claim: The cerebral representations of auditory and visual speech are mediated by both modality-specific and overlapping (potentially amodal) representations.
source: Our results show that the cerebral representations of auditory and visual speech are mediated by both modality-specific and overlapping (potentially amodal) representations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Several parietal, temporal and frontal regions were engaged in the encoding of both acoustically and visually conveyed word identities.
source: While several parietal, temporal and frontal regions were engaged in the encoding of both acoustically and visually conveyed word identities ('stimulus classification'), comprehension in both sensory modalities was driven mostly by distinct networks.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the stimulus classification results.

claim: Comprehension in both sensory modalities was driven mostly by distinct networks.
source: While several parietal, temporal and frontal regions were engaged in the encoding of both acoustically and visually conveyed word identities ('stimulus classification'), comprehension in both sensory modalities was driven mostly by distinct networks.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neurobehavioral prediction results.

claim: Only the inferior frontal and anterior angular gyrus contained adjacent regions that contributed to both auditory and visual comprehension.
source: Only the inferior frontal and anterior angular gyrus contained adjacent regions that contributed to both auditory and visual comprehension.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neurobehavioral prediction results.

claim: Auditory and visual cortices represent strongly modality-specific word identities.
source: On the other hand, auditory and visual cortices represent strongly modality-specific word identities.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the stimulus classification results.

claim: Anterior angular and inferior frontal regions facilitate both auditory and visual comprehension.
source: Second, it is also supported by the observation that anterior angular and inferior frontal regions facilitate both auditory and visual comprehension, while distinct regions support modality-specific comprehension.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neurobehavioral prediction results.

claim: Middle occipital and posterior angular representations specifically drive auditory comprehension.
source: In particular, our data suggest that middle occipital and posterior angular representations specifically drive auditory comprehension.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neurobehavioral prediction results.

claim: Superior frontal and temporal regions are engaged in lip reading.
source: In addition, superior frontal and temporal regions are engaged in lip reading, although we did not find strong evidence for a modality preference of these regions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neurobehavioral prediction results.

claim: None of the comprehension-relevant regions was strictly lateralised.
source: None of these comprehension-relevant regions was strictly lateralised, in line with the notion that speech comprehension is largely a bilateral process (Kennedy-Higgins et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a result from the lateralisation test, supported by a citation.

claim: The inability to cross-classify auditory and visual speech from local activity supports the conclusion that the nature of local representations of acoustic and visual speech is relatively distinct.
source: The inability to cross-classify auditory and visual speech from local activity further supports the conclusion that the nature of local representations of acoustic and visual speech is relatively distinct.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cross-classification results.

claim: Local activity could encode a given word based on acoustic or visual evidence but using distinct activity patterns.
source: It could be that local activity encodes a given word based on acoustic or visual evidence but using distinct activity patterns.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the cross-classification results.

claim: The activity patterns by which auditory and visual speech are encoded may be partly distinct, even within regions that represent both acoustically and visually mediated word information.
source: Our results hence provide evidence that the activity patterns by which auditory and visual speech are encoded may be partly distinct, even within regions that represent both acoustically and visually mediated word information, such as the inferior frontal and anterior angular gyrus.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cross-classification results.

claim: The stimulus-domain classifier used may also capture processes potentially related to attention or motor preparation.
source: This suggests that the stimulus-domain classifier used here may also capture processes potentially related to attention or motor preparation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the widespread classification results.

claim: The segregation of comprehension-relevant auditory and visual representations provides a possible explanation for the finding that auditory or verbal skills and visual lip reading are uncorrelated in normal-hearing adults.
source: The segregation of comprehension-relevant auditory and visual representations provides a possible explanation for the finding that auditory or verbal skills and visual lip reading are uncorrelated in normal-hearing adults (Jeffers and Barley, 1980; Mohammed et al., 2006; Summerfield, 1992).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results, supported by citations to previous behavioral studies.

claim: Individual differences in lip reading represent something other than normal variation in speech perceptual abilities.
source: Indeed, it has been suggested that individual differences in lip reading represent something other than normal variation in speech perceptual abilities (Summerfield, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Lip reading skills are unrelated to reading abilities in the typical adult population.
source: For example, lip reading skills are unrelated to reading abilities in the typical adult population (Arnold and Köpsel, 1996; Mohammed et al., 2006), although a relationship is sometimes found in deaf or dyslexic children (Arnold and Köpsel, 1996; de Gelder and Vroomen, 1998; Kyle et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Visual speech may activate many regions in an unspecific manner, without engaging specific semantic or lexical representations, maybe as a result of attentional engagement or feed-back.
source: Hence, it could be that visual speech may activate many regions in an unspecific manner, without engaging specific semantic or lexical representations, maybe as a result of attentional engagement or feed-back (Balk et al., 2013; Ozker et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: Auditory cortical areas are equally activated by visual words and pseudo-words.
source: Support for this interpretation comes from lip reading studies showing that auditory cortical areas are equally activated by visual words and pseudo-words (Calvert, 1997; Paulesu et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Studies demonstrate cross-modal activations in early sensory regions also for simplistic stimuli.
source: and studies demonstrating cross-modal activations in early sensory regions also for simplistic stimuli (Ferraro et al., 2020; Ibrahim et al., 2016; Petro et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Visual speech comprehension is mediated by parietal and inferior frontal regions that likely contribute to both auditory and visual speech comprehension, but also engage superior temporal and superior frontal regions.
source: Our results suggest that visual speech comprehension is mediated by parietal and inferior frontal regions that likely contribute to both auditory and visual speech comprehension, but also engage superior temporal and superior frontal regions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The results support a route of visual speech into auditory cortical and temporal regions.
source: Thereby our results support a route of visual speech into auditory cortical and temporal regions but provide no evidence for an overlap of speech representations in the temporal lobe that would facilitate both lip-reading and acoustic speech comprehension, in contrast to recent suggestions from a lesion-based approach (Hickok et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results, contrasted with a citation to previous research.

claim: The results provide no evidence for an overlap of speech representations in the temporal lobe that would facilitate both lip-reading and acoustic speech comprehension.
source: Thereby our results support a route of visual speech into auditory cortical and temporal regions but provide no evidence for an overlap of speech representations in the temporal lobe that would facilitate both lip-reading and acoustic speech comprehension, in contrast to recent suggestions from a lesion-based approach (Hickok et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results, contrasted with a citation to previous research.

claim: The IFG and the anterior angular gyrus facilitate both auditory and visual speech comprehension.
source: Our results suggest that these facilitate both auditory and visual speech comprehension, in line with previous suggestions (Simanova et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results, supported by a citation.

claim: Previous work has implicated the IFG and anterior angular gyrus in the visual facilitation of auditory speech-in-noise perception and lip-reading itself.
source: Previous work has also implicated these regions in the visual facilitation of auditory speech-in-noise perception (Giordano et al., 2017) and lip-reading itself (Bourguignon et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Lip-reading drives the improvement of speech perception in noise.
source: Behavioural studies have shown that lip-reading drives the improvement of speech perception in noise (Macleod and Summerfield, 1987)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The representations of visual speech in the IFG and anterior angular gyrus may be central for hearing in noisy environments.
source: hence suggesting that the representations of visual speech in these regions may be central for hearing in noisy environments.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results and previous behavioral studies.

claim: The IFG and anterior angular gyrus in the present study resemble the left-lateralised dorsal pathway activated in deaf signers when seeing signed verbs.
source: Interestingly, these regions resemble the left-lateralised dorsal pathway activated in deaf signers when seeing signed verbs (Emmorey et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous research, supported by a citation.

claim: Acoustic comprehension was related to occipital brain activity.
source: We also found that acoustic comprehension was related to occipital brain activity (c.f. Figure 3).
evidence: This is a result from the neurobehavioral analysis, shown in Figure 3.

claim: Salient sounds activate visual cortices.
source: Previous work has shown that salient sounds activate visual cortices (Feng et al., 2014; McDonald et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Top-down projections provide visual regions with semantic information, for example about object categories.
source: with top-down projections providing visual regions with semantic information, for example about object categories (Petro et al., 2017; Revina et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Attention may have automatically facilitated the entrance of top-down semantic information into occipital regions that, in a multisensory context, would encode the lip-movement trajectory.
source: Attention may therefore have automatically facilitated the entrance of top-down semantic information into occipital regions that, in a multisensory context, would encode the lip-movement trajectory, in order to maximise task performance (McDonald et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the occipital activity during auditory comprehension, supported by a citation.

claim: The lack of significant cross-classification performance suggests that the nature of the top-down induced representation differs from that induced by direct lip-movement information.
source: The lack of significant cross-classification performance suggests that the nature of this top-down induced representation differs from that induced by direct lip-movement information.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cross-classification results.

claim: At the single neuron level some studies have proposed that only those neurons encoding the specific stimulus optimally are driving behaviour.
source: At the single neuron level some studies have proposed that only those neurons encoding the specific stimulus optimally are driving behaviour (Britten et al., 1996; Pitkow et al., 2015; Purushothaman and Bradley, 2005; Tsunada et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Some studies suggest that 'plain' sensory information and sensory information predictive of choice can be decoupled across neurons.
source: while others suggest that 'plain' sensory information and sensory information predictive of choice can be decoupled across neurons (Runyan et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The intersection of brain activity predictive of stimulus and choice is difficult to quantify for high-dimensional data.
source: While theoretically attractive, this intersection is difficult to quantify for high-dimensional data, in part as direct estimates of this intersection, for example based on information-theoretic approaches, are computationally costly (Pica et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous methodological work.

claim: Brain regions allowing for a sub-optimal read-out of the actual stimulus are predictive of the perceptual outcome, whereas those areas allowing the best read-out not necessarily predict behaviour.
source: Although one has to be careful in interpreting this as causally driving behaviour, our results reveal that brain regions allowing for a sub-optimal read-out of the actual stimulus are predictive of the perceptual outcome, whereas those areas allowing the best read-out not necessarily predict behaviour.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: This dissociation between stimulus encoding and behavioral prediction is emerging in several recent studies on the neural basis underlying perception.
source: This dissociation is emerging in several recent studies on the neural basis underlying perception (Bouton et al., 2018; Grootswagers et al., 2018; Hasson et al., 2007; Keitel et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Networks mediating speech comprehension can neither be understood by mapping speech representations during passive perception nor during task performance, if the analysis itself is not geared towards directly revealing the perception-relevant representations.

claim: Each target word appeared in 10 different auditory and visual sentences.
source: The 18 target words, which always occurred in the third or second last position of the sentence, each appeared in 10 different auditory and visual sentences to facilitate the use of classification-based data analysis (see table in Supplementary file 1 for all used target words).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The signal-to-noise ratio across participants ranged from −7.75 dB to −3.97 dB (−5.96 ± 1.06 dB [M ± SD]).
source: The signal-to-noise ratio across participants ranged from −7.75 dB to −3.97 dB (−5.96 ± 1.06 dB [M ± SD]; see Figure 1B).

claim: MEG was recorded with a 248-magnetometers, whole-head MEG system at a sampling rate of 1 KHz.
source: MEG was recorded with a 248-magnetometers, whole-head MEG system (MAGNES 3600 WH, 4-D Neuroimaging) at a sampling rate of 1 KHz.

claim: Source reconstruction was performed using Fieldtrip, SPM8, and the Freesurfer toolbox.
source: Source reconstruction was performed using Fieldtrip, SPM8, and the Freesurfer toolbox.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis method.

claim: A forward solution was computed using a single-shell model.
source: A forward solution was computed using a single-shell model (Nolte, 2003).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis method, supported by a citation.

claim: Sensor-level timeseries were projected into source space using a frequency-specific linear constraint minimum variance (LCMV) beamformer.
source: We projected sensor-level timeseries into source space using a frequency-specific linear constraint minimum variance (LCMV) beamformer (Van Veen et al., 1997) with a regularisation parameter of 7% and optimal dipole orientation (singular value decomposition method).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis method, supported by a citation.

claim: Grid points had a spacing of 6 mm, resulting in 12,337 points covering the whole brain.
source: Grid points had a spacing of 6 mm, resulting in 12,337 points covering the whole brain.
evidence: This is a description of the source space grid.

claim: 6490 grid points corresponding to cortical regions were selected for subsequent analyses.
source: For subsequent analyses, we selected grid points that corresponded to cortical regions only (parcellated using the AAL atlas; Tzourio-Mazoyer et al., 2002). This resulted in 6490 grid points in total.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis method, supported by a citation.

claim: Multi-variate single-trial classification was used to localise cerebral representations of the target words in source activity.
source: We used multi-variate single-trial classification to localise cerebral representations of the target words in source activity (Grootswagers et al., 2017; Guggenmos et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis method, supported by citations.

claim: The 500 ms of activity following the onset of each target word was extracted and re-binned at 20 ms resolution.
source: We extracted the 500 ms of activity following the onset of each target word and re-binned the source activity at 20 ms resolution.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis method.

claim: Classification was performed on spatial searchlights of 1.2 cm radius.
source: Classification was performed on spatial searchlights of 1.2 cm radius.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis method.

claim: The typical searchlight contained 31 neighbours (median value), with 95% of searchlights containing 17 to 33 grid points.
source: The typical searchlight contained 31 neighbours (median value), with 95% of searchlights containing 17 to 33 grid points.

claim: A correlation-based nearest-neighbour classifier was selected as it performed slightly better than other classifiers.
source: We initially tested a number of different classifiers, including linear-discriminant and diagonal-linear classifiers, and then selected a correlation-based nearest-neighbour classifier as this performed slightly better than the others (although we note that the difference in peak classification performance was only on the range of 2–3% between different classifiers).
evidence: This is a description of the classifier selection process.

claim: Linear classifiers were focused on because they have been shown to often perform equally well than more complex non-linear classifiers, while also offering insights that are more readily interpretable.
source: We focussed on linear classifiers here because these have been shown to often perform equally well than more complex non-linear classifiers, while also offering insights that are more readily interpretable (Haxby et al., 2014; Kamitani and Tong, 2005; Ritchie et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a justification for the choice of classifier, supported by citations.

claim: The representational distance was defined as the average correlation with trials of the same word identity minus the mean of the correlation with the three alternatives.
source: This representational distance was defined as the average correlation with trials of the same (within-target distances) word identity minus the mean of the correlation with the three alternatives (between-target distances; see Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis method.

claim: The statistical relation between participants performance and single-trial representational distances was quantified using a regularised logistic regression.
source: We then quantified the statistical relation between participants performance (accuracy) and these single-trial representational distances (Cichy et al., 2017; Grootswagers et al., 2018; Panzeri et al., 2017; Pica et al., 2017; Ritchie et al., 2015). This analysis was based on a regularised logistic regression (Parra et al., 2005)
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis method, supported by citations.

claim: Pairwise phonological distances for the stimulus material were computed using Phonological Corpus Tools.
source: For each pair of words we computed their phonological distance using the Phonological Corpus Tools (V1.4.0) based on the phonetic string similarity ('phonological edit distance') derived from the transcription tier, using the Irvine Phonotactic Online Dictionary (Vaden et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis method, supported by a citation.

claim: Semantic distances were computed using the fastTExt vector representation of English words.
source: We also computed pairwise semantic distances using the fastTExt vector representation of English words trained on Common Crawl and Wikipedia obtained online (file cc.en.300.vec) (Grave et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis method, supported by a citation.

claim: Cluster-based permutation was used to correct for multiple comparisons.
source: Cluster-based permutation was used to correct for multiple comparisons (Maris and Oostenveld, 2007).
evidence: This is a description of the statistical method, supported by a citation.

claim: Significant clusters were identified based on a first-level significance derived from the 99.95th percentile of the permuted distribution (family-wise error [FWE] of p=0.001).
source: Significant clusters were identified based on a first-level significance derived from the 99.95th percentile of the permuted distribution (family-wise error [FWE] of p=0.001), using the summed statistics (Tsum) across grid points within a cluster, and by requiring a minimal cluster size of 10 grid points.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical method.
